rationale: This prospective open-label pilot evaluates psilocybin-assisted therapy for mood dysfunction in 12 people with Parkinson disease. Current psychosis involving loss of insight was an exclusion, while minor and major hallucination scores were recorded in baseline clinical characterization. The study intervention and psychosis safety context do not give a dried fig or exposure-specific hallucination comparison.

The prospective cohort followed people with baseline minor phenomena, including illusions, feelings of presence and passage hallucinations. Of 38 recruited, 34 entered the primary analysis and 24 developed psychosis during follow-up. Time to onset on the MDS-UPDRS and enhanced SAPS-PD is a composite incident outcome, with no dried fig intake measurement or food-specific visual episode rate.

The retrospective case series follows Parkinson dopamine dysregulation around pallidal stimulation. Five of six patients had preoperative psychosis, most commonly visual hallucinations described in the context of high dopaminergic doses. The recorded clinical and drug course is a separate exposure and provides no dried fig comparison.

The investigators compare lower-limb vibration and gait or cortical outcomes in Parkinson disease. Visual hallucinations appear in the discussion of other nonmotor presentations. The assessed outcomes concern gait freezing and electrophysiology and do not include a dietary visual episode comparison.

ATPARK plans collection of food habits and environmental risk factors, along with longitudinal clinical phenotyping across atypical parkinsonism syndromes. Visual hallucinations appear in the literature discussion of phenotypes. The protocol does not identify a dried fig item or an outcome estimate linked to food intake.

The retrospective multicenter comparison studies cognition in non-demented Parkinson participants with and without GBA variants. Hallucinations were among nonmotor characteristics assessed and appear in interpretation of phenotype differences. The comparisons are defined by genotype and cognition, without dried fig exposure or a food-associated change in visual episode frequency.

The article assesses the Dementia Cognitive Fluctuation Scale in people with Parkinson disease without dementia. The investigators distinguish fluctuations of attention or arousal and discuss visual hallucinations as part of the clinical background. Scale performance and correlates are separate from the effect of eating dried figs on visual hallucinations.

The report follows visual hallucinations and cognitive changes in a case of hyperammonemia with vascular shunts. Embolization addresses the clinical source of the encephalopathy. The diagnosis, exposure and outcome timing do not establish a Parkinson food comparison.

Susceptibility mapping compares imaging patterns among dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson disease dementia, Parkinson disease and controls. Hallucinations help characterize Lewy body phenotypes. Imaging group differences provide no dried fig exposure or visual episode rate by food intake.

A deep brain stimulation report considers absent subthalamic activity during microelectrode recording and the diagnostic differential. Visual hallucinations appear in discussion of Parkinson disease and progressive supranuclear palsy. No fig intake or measured visual outcome informs that comparison.

Healthy participants received tested and reference formulations of amantadine under fasting conditions. The article discusses prior visual hallucination adverse events in clinical use, and its own comparisons concern drug exposure and safety. Fasting is a controlled condition and the paper has no dried fig or Parkinson hallucination comparison.

A post hoc HARMONY subgroup analysis evaluates continued pimavanserin versus randomized withdrawal in selected responders with Parkinson disease dementia or dementia with Lewy bodies. Relapse occurred in 1 of 19 continuing drug and 11 of 20 on placebo in the interim efficacy set. The endpoint combines hallucinations and delusions with other relapse criteria, and there is no food exposure. The subgroup is part of NCT03325556.

The study quantifies cerebrospinal fluid alpha-synuclein seed activity through endpoint dilution. It compares assay estimates by baseline symptoms, including visual hallucination status. The clinical comparison is presence rather than frequency or a response to an exposure, and dried fig intake was not measured.

A clinical case had visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition and parkinsonian features. Neuropathology identified argyrophilic grain disease in a Lewy body dementia mimic. In this paper grains describes neuropathology. There is no dried fig exposure.

The randomized trial tests home-based transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation and assesses clinical, autonomic and brain measures. The intervention is a stimulation device, registered as ChiCTR2300070828. The original body offers no prepared fig exposure or corresponding visual hallucination frequency outcome.

The series links caregiver-recorded cognitive fluctuations in four people with Parkinson disease dementia to immediately preceding low blood pressure on ambulatory monitoring. Meal timing appears in the plots and the authors propose more detailed food documentation in future studies. Visual hallucinations are recorded in case histories, rather than as the events associated with meals. No fig is identified and the study gives no comparable visual episode frequency.

A pilot in Lewy body disorders uses immersive scenes, eye tracking and verbal descriptions to distinguish visual hallucinations from misperceptions and ordinary perceptions. Its laboratory event counts are compared with clinical history groups in eleven participants. Elicited events under ambiguous visual conditions do not measure daily episodes after eating dried figs.

Three cases of sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease are described. Visual phenomena or hallucinations appear in individual clinical histories along with cognitive and movement changes. The source supplies neither a Parkinson food exposure nor an appropriate outcome comparison.

The DREAMER protocol plans a cohort for isolated REM sleep without atonia and tracks possible evolving clinical signs, including visual hallucinations. It provides a collection framework, not observed symptom change after a dietary exposure. NCT06140511 is its linked registration.

The open-label phase 1/2 study evaluates transplantation of stem-cell-derived dopaminergic cells. An individual visual-hallucination event is reported after a medication adjustment during follow-up. The study records a transplant and medication safety chronology, without measuring dried fig exposure or an episode rate for that exposure.

A case follows visual misperceptions and then predominant somatic infestation sensations during continuous foslevodopa and foscarbidopa infusion. Earlier visual hallucinations appeared with another dopaminergic treatment. The history distinguishes modalities and medication periods and gives no dried fig exposure or food-specific visual episode frequency.
